long.title: My favourite place to relax
long.text:
A  Lena
There is a small lake near my town, and I go there on Sunday mornings when it is quiet. I usually take a book and sit under a big tree. Sometimes my brother comes with me and we go fishing, but we never catch much! In winter it is too cold, so I go to the library instead. The best thing about the lake is that it is free.
B  Tom
My favourite place is my grandmother's garden. She grows vegetables and lots of flowers, and I help her every Saturday. We often cook lunch together with the vegetables we pick. It takes me forty minutes to get there by bus, but I don't mind because I listen to music on the way. My friends think gardening is boring, but I find it relaxing.

I relax at the swimming pool in the city centre. I go three times a week, usually in the evening after work. It costs five pounds each time, which is quite expensive, so I want to buy a monthly ticket. After swimming I always feel tired but happy. I sometimes meet my friend Kim there and we have a coffee in the café.

long.text:
A  Nick
My first job was in a bookshop when I was seventeen. I worked there every Saturday for a year. I put new books on the shelves and helped customers find what they wanted. The manager was quite strict, but I learned a lot from her. The pay wasn't very good, but I could buy books cheaply, which I loved because I read a lot.

When I was sixteen, I got a summer job at a hotel by the sea. I cleaned rooms in the morning and worked in the restaurant in the evening. It was hard work and I was always tired, but I made some great friends. We often went to the beach together after work. I also practised my English because many of the guests came from other countries.

My first job was delivering newspapers in my neighbourhood. I had to get up at five o'clock every morning before school, even in winter when it was dark and cold. I used my bike, so I got very fit! I did the job for two years and saved enough money to buy my first computer. My parents were surprised that I never missed a day.

long.title: A Year Without a Car
long.text:
When my old car finally broke down last January, the mechanic told me that repairing it would cost more than the car was worth. I was annoyed at first, because I had driven to work every day for ten years. But my sister suggested an experiment: why not try living without a car for a whole year? I laughed at the idea, but I agreed to try it for one month.
The first week was difficult. My office is eight kilometres from my flat, and I had to work out which buses to take. On the second day I got on the wrong one and arrived forty minutes late. My boss was not pleased. However, by the end of the week I had found a route that took only ten minutes longer than driving, and I could read on the bus instead of sitting in traffic.
After a month, I noticed some surprising changes. I was walking about six thousand more steps a day, and I slept better than I had for years. I was also saving money. Without paying for petrol, parking and insurance, I had almost two hundred dollars more each month. So I decided to continue the experiment.
Of course, there were problems. Shopping became more complicated, and I had to plan carefully before I went to the supermarket. Visiting my parents, who live in a village with only two buses a day, was the hardest part. A couple of times I had to borrow my sister's car, which she reminded me about often.
Now the year is over, and people keep asking me whether I will buy a new car. I'm still not sure. I miss the freedom of being able to go anywhere at any time, especially at weekends. But I don't miss the traffic or the cost. For now, I've bought a second-hand bicycle, and I've joined a car-sharing club for the occasional long journey. Perhaps that is the right balance for me.

long.title: Learning on the Job
long.text:
Most cafés hire staff who already know how to make coffee and serve customers. The Green Door café in Hue does the opposite. Every one of its waiters, cooks and baristas is a young person who has never had a job before. The café is part of a training programme for teenagers who left school early, and after six months there, most of them go on to find work in hotels and restaurants.
The idea came from Minh Chau, a former hotel manager. 'When I was interviewing people for jobs, I met so many young people who were clever and hard-working but had no experience,' she explains. 'Nobody wanted to give them a chance, so they couldn't get experience. I wanted to break that circle.'
Trainees spend their mornings in a classroom above the café, where they study English, food safety and customer service. In the afternoons they work downstairs with real customers. Mistakes happen, of course. 'On my first day I dropped a whole tray of drinks,' laughs Nam, who is seventeen. 'I wanted to run away. But the customers were really kind, and my trainer showed me how to carry the tray properly.'
Customers seem happy to be part of the project. Many of them are tourists who have read about the café online, but there are also local office workers who come in every day. A small notice on each table explains the programme and asks customers to be patient. 'The coffee is excellent and the service is friendly,' says one regular customer. 'If it's a bit slow sometimes, I don't mind at all.'
The café does not make much profit, and it depends on donations to pay for the classes. Minh Chau admits that money is a constant worry. But she has no plans to give up. Last year, forty-two trainees finished the programme, and thirty-eight of them are now in full-time jobs. 'That number,' she says, 'is the only profit I really care about.'

long.title: Evening and weekend courses
long.text:
A  Riverside Cooking School
Learn to cook simple meals from around the world in our friendly kitchen. Classes are on Tuesday evenings and are suitable for complete beginners. You take home everything you make. The course lasts ten weeks and all ingredients are included in the price.
B  City Photography Club
Improve your photos with an experienced photographer. We meet every Saturday morning and visit a different part of the city each week. You need your own camera, but it doesn't have to be expensive; many members use their phones. Free for students.
C  Spanish for Travellers
A short, practical course for people who are going on holiday soon. In four evening lessons you'll learn how to order food, ask for directions and book a hotel room. Groups have no more than eight people, and online lessons are also available.
D  Hilltop Pottery Studio
Make your own cups, bowls and plates on our pottery wheels. We run weekend courses for adults with or without experience. We fire your work in our oven and you can collect it a week later. Please wear old clothes!
E  Get Fit Together
A course for people who want to get fit but hate gyms. We exercise outdoors in the park every Sunday morning, whatever the weather. Each session includes running, games and stretching. Bring a friend for free on your first visit.
F  First Steps in Coding
Build your own website in six weeks. You don't need any experience, but you must bring a laptop. Lessons are on Wednesday evenings at the public library, and our teachers are all professional software developers.
G  Creative Writing Workshop
Write stories and poems and share them with a small, friendly group. Each Thursday evening we read work by famous writers and then try their techniques ourselves. At the end of the course, the best stories are published in a small book.
H  Guitar for Beginners
Learn to play your favourite songs in just eight weeks. Lessons take place on Monday evenings, and guitars are provided, so you don't need to buy one. Classes are relaxed and fun, and there's no need to read music.

long.title: Books to read
long.text:
A  The Silent Forest
A thriller set in a dark Canadian forest, where a young detective searches for a missing scientist. The story moves fast and every chapter ends with a surprise. At over 500 pages, it is a long read, but most readers can't put it down.
B  Kitchen Stories
Part cookbook, part family history. The writer shares her grandmother's recipes from Vietnam together with stories about growing up in a busy restaurant. The recipes are simple and the photos are beautiful.

An experienced athlete explains how anyone can train for their first marathon. Clear weekly plans, advice on food and sleep, and honest stories about the writer's own mistakes make this a practical guide.
D  Stars Above Us
A short, easy introduction to astronomy for teenagers. Colourful pictures and simple diagrams explain the planets, the stars and how telescopes work. Each chapter is only a few pages long.
E  The Last Summer
A gentle, funny novel about three old friends who spend one last summer together in a seaside town. Nothing very dramatic happens, but the characters are wonderful and the ending is moving.
F  Money Made Simple
A clear guide to managing your money, written for young people starting their first job. It explains saving, bank accounts and how to avoid debt without using complicated language.
G  Lost Cities
The true story of the archaeologists who discovered ancient cities in the jungle. Full of adventure and real photographs, it reads like a novel, but every word is true.

A collection of short, funny stories that you can read in five minutes each. It is perfect for reading on the bus or before bed, and a great present for anyone who needs cheering up.

long.title: My Year as a Volunteer
long.text:
After I finished school, I didn't know what I wanted to study at university, so I decided to take a year off. My parents were worried that I would waste the time, but a friend of my mother's told me about a project that needed volunteers to help in a small library in the mountains in the north of the country. I had never lived away from home before, and I wasn't sure I would be any good at it, but I agreed to go for six months.

The first few weeks were difficult. The village was much colder than I had expected, and I had brought the wrong clothes. The library was just one room in the old school, and most of the books were in very bad condition. On my first day only two children came in, and they left after ten minutes because there was nothing they wanted to read.

I realised that I had to do more than sit behind a desk. I started a reading club on Saturday mornings and asked the children what they would like to read. Most of them wanted comics and books about animals, which the library didn't have. So I wrote to publishers and bookshops in the city, and to my surprise several of them sent boxes of books for free. Soon the room was full every weekend, and some parents began to come too.

In the end I stayed for a whole year instead of six months. When I left, the village organised a small party for me, and one of the girls from the reading club gave me a card that said she wanted to be a teacher. That was the moment I knew what I wanted to do with my own life. I'm now in my second year of a teaching degree, and I still visit the village every summer.

long.title: Why We Put Things Off
long.text:
For years I believed that I was simply lazy. I would sit down to write a report, check my emails 'just once', and look up two hours later having achieved nothing except a tidy inbox. So I was relieved, and slightly surprised, when a psychologist friend told me that procrastination has very little to do with laziness. 'Lazy people don't feel guilty about doing nothing,' she pointed out. 'Procrastinators feel terrible. That's the whole problem.'
According to researchers, procrastination is better understood as a problem of managing emotions than of managing time. When we face a task that makes us feel anxious, bored or uncertain, putting it off brings immediate relief. The bad feeling disappears, at least for a while, and our brains learn that avoiding the task is rewarding. The next time, the temptation to delay is even stronger. Unfortunately, the relief never lasts. The deadline gets closer, the anxiety returns, and it is usually worse than before.
Perfectionism makes matters worse. People who believe that every piece of work must be flawless often find it hardest to begin, because starting means risking a result that falls short of their own standards. As long as the task remains untouched, it can still, in theory, be perfect. Researchers have found that perfectionists are no more likely than anyone else to produce excellent work; they are simply more likely to produce it late, or not at all. Ironically, the fear of doing something badly is frequently what prevents people from doing it well.
This explains why the most popular advice often fails. Making detailed to-do lists or buying a new diary may feel productive, but it does nothing about the uncomfortable feeling at the heart of the problem. In fact, planning can itself become a form of delay: I once spent an entire afternoon designing a colour-coded timetable for a project I then failed to start.
So what does work? One technique that researchers recommend is surprisingly simple: make the first step so small that it is almost impossible to refuse. Instead of telling yourself to 'write the report', you decide to open the document and write one sentence. Once we have started, the task usually seems less threatening, and we often carry on far longer than we planned. Psychologists call this lowering the 'activation energy' of a task. A version of the same idea is to agree to work on something for just ten minutes, with full permission to stop when the time is up. Most people, it turns out, don't stop.
Another approach is to be kinder to ourselves. It sounds like the opposite of what a procrastinator needs, but a study of university students found that those who forgave themselves for putting off revision before one exam procrastinated less before the next. Self-criticism, it seems, simply adds to the negative emotions that caused the delay in the first place.
I have been trying both techniques for the past three months, with mixed results. The 'one sentence' rule has been genuinely useful, and this article is proof: I began it with a single line at seven o'clock this morning. Forgiving myself has been harder. Years of telling myself off are not easily undone, and I still catch myself calling myself names when I miss a deadline. But I no longer believe I am lazy, and that, oddly, has made it easier to get things done.

long.title: Starting Again: Four Career Changers
long.text:
A  Hoa, former bank manager, now a baker
'I spent fifteen years at the bank and, honestly, I was good at my job. The money was excellent, and I never imagined leaving. Then my mother became ill, and I took six months off to look after her. During that time I started baking bread every morning, mostly to keep myself calm. When it was time to go back to work, I just couldn't face it. My husband thought I'd lost my mind, and for the first year he was probably right: I was working twice as many hours for a third of the income. Things are more stable now. I've got four employees and a waiting list for my sourdough. I still miss the certainty of a monthly salary, though.'
B  David, former lawyer, now a secondary school teacher
'People assume I left law because I hated it, but that isn't true. I enjoyed the puzzles, the arguments, even the long hours. What I didn't enjoy was the feeling that my work only mattered to a few very rich clients. I'd always helped out at a youth club at weekends, and I realised that those few hours were the best part of my week. Retraining took a year, and it was humbling to be a student again at thirty-eight, surrounded by people half my age. Teaching is far more tiring than I expected. A day with thirty teenagers takes more energy than any court case did. But I've never once regretted the change.'
C  Linh, former engineer, now an organic farmer
'My decision was carefully planned. I didn't just wake up one morning and buy a farm. For three years I spent every holiday working on other people's farms, learning what the job actually involved, and I saved as much of my salary as I could. When I finally bought the land, I already had a business plan and a list of restaurants interested in my vegetables. My engineering background has turned out to be surprisingly useful. I designed my own irrigation system, which uses forty per cent less water than the one the previous owner had installed. The hardest thing has been the weather. You can plan everything, and then a single storm destroys a month's work.'
D  Marco, former chef, now a software developer
'Kitchens are exciting, but they're also hot, loud and exhausting, and after twenty years my back was telling me to stop. I'd always been curious about computers, so I signed up for an online coding course, just to see whether I had any ability. It turned out I did. The course was free, which was lucky, because I couldn't have afforded anything else at the time. Getting my first job was hard: many companies weren't interested in someone without a degree. In the end, a restaurant booking company hired me because I understood their customers better than anyone else in the office. These days I cook purely for pleasure, and I enjoy it far more than I used to.'

long.title: The Secret Life of Lost Property
long.text:
Every day, thousands of people leave something behind on a train, a bus or an underground platform. Umbrellas are the most common items, followed by phones, bags and, more surprisingly, single shoes. Most of these objects end up in a lost property office, and the one I visited last month, which serves a large city's transport network, receives around a thousand items every single day.

The office is in a basement beneath one of the main stations, and it looks more like a warehouse than an office. Long rows of shelves stretch into the distance, each labelled with a date. Items are kept for three months; if nobody claims them, they are sold at auction or given to charity. 'People think we're a place where things go to be forgotten,' says Maria, who has worked there for eleven years. 'But we reunite a lot of people with things that really matter to them.'

Technology has changed the job considerably. Until recently, staff wrote a description of each item by hand, and anyone who had lost something had to come in person or phone and describe it. Now every item is photographed and entered into an online database, and the system automatically suggests matches when someone reports a loss. As a result, the proportion of items returned to their owners has almost doubled in five years.

The work follows a strict routine. Each morning, everything collected from trains and stations the night before arrives in large plastic boxes. Staff sort the items into categories, attach a numbered label and record exactly where and when each one was found, which can be vital when two people claim the same object. Valuable items such as jewellery and cash are counted twice, by two different members of staff, and kept in a safe until their owners appear.

Some of the objects that arrive are remarkable. Maria has seen a stuffed bear wearing a crown, a full set of false teeth and, on one occasion, a wedding dress still in its bag. 'The bride came for it the next morning,' she tells me, 'two days before the wedding. She cried when she saw it.' The strangest item she remembers is a small boat, which someone apparently carried onto a late-night train and then forgot.

Not everything is so charming. Staff must deal with a lot of food left in bags, and phones and laptops require special care because of the personal information they contain. Electronic devices are locked in a separate room, and anyone claiming one has to prove that it belongs to them, usually by unlocking it in front of a member of staff.

What strikes me most is how emotional the work can be. A lost umbrella is easily replaced, but a bag containing a family photograph or a notebook full of someone's writing is not. Maria says the best part of the job is the moment when people realise they are going to get their belongings back. 'You see the relief on their faces,' she says. 'For a few seconds, they forget whatever else is worrying them.'

long.title: Learning to Fly at Fifty
long.text:
For most of my adult life I told people that I would learn to fly 'one day'. It was the kind of ambition that is easy to keep because you never have to test it. I had a demanding job, two children and a mortgage, and flying lessons seemed both expensive and slightly ridiculous for someone like me. Then, a few weeks after my fiftieth birthday, my daughter gave me a voucher for a trial lesson at a small airfield outside the city. 'You keep talking about it,' she said. 'Now you have to do it.'

I expected the instructor to be a young former air force pilot. In fact Joan was sixty-three and had started flying herself at the age of forty-five, after her children had left home. She spent the first half hour on the ground, walking me round the aircraft and explaining the checks that every pilot makes before take-off. I was impatient to get into the air, but I later realised that this was the most important lesson of all: in flying, preparation is everything.

When we finally took off, Joan let me hold the controls almost immediately. What surprised me was not the view, although that was beautiful, but how much the small plane moved in the wind. I gripped the controls so tightly that my hands ached. Joan told me, gently, that the aircraft would fly itself quite happily if I let it, and that my job was to make small corrections rather than fight it.

I signed up for a full course that afternoon. The next eighteen months were harder than I had imagined. The written exams covered weather, navigation and air law, and I had not sat an exam since university. There were weeks when bad weather cancelled every lesson, and I began to wonder whether I was too old to learn something so new. Several times I considered giving up. What kept me going was the moment, about halfway through, when I made my first landing without Joan touching the controls.

Flying also changed the way I organised my life. Lessons had to be booked around the weather, which meant checking forecasts obsessively and keeping my weekends free. My husband joked that he had lost me to the sky, yet he came to the airfield more often than he would admit, and eventually he took a trial lesson himself. At work, colleagues who had never shown much interest in my private life started asking every Monday whether I had been up in the air.

I passed my final test last spring. I now fly about once a month, usually with a friend who shares the cost. I am not a natural pilot, and I never will be, but I have discovered that being careful and methodical matters far more than talent. Perhaps the most valuable thing flying has taught me has nothing to do with aircraft: it is that the excuses we make for not trying things are usually more frightening than the things themselves.

long.title: Starting Young: Four Entrepreneurs
long.text:
A  Jade, 23, runs a company that sells second-hand clothes online
I started by selling my own old clothes to pay for a holiday, and I was amazed how quickly they sold. Within a year I had a small warehouse and two employees. The hardest part was learning to say no: friends kept asking me to stock things that didn't fit the business. My advice is to know exactly who your customers are. I still check every item myself before it goes online, because one bad review can cost you dozens of sales. These days I spend more time on photography and packaging than on buying stock, because presentation is what customers notice first. I'd like to open a real shop one day, but rents in my city are far too high at the moment.
B  Sam, 25, makes and sells skateboards
My parents thought I was wasting my time, which made me more determined to prove them wrong. I had no money, so I borrowed tools from a local workshop and built the first boards in my garage. My biggest mistake was growing too fast: I took on a huge order from a shop chain, couldn't deliver on time and nearly went bankrupt. Now I grow slowly and only promise what I know I can do. Each board takes about six hours to make by hand, and no two are exactly the same. Some of my customers are professional skaters, which still amazes me.
C  Nadia, 22, has developed a language-learning app
I built the first version of the app while I was still at university, mainly to help my grandmother learn English. A lecturer encouraged me to enter a competition for student businesses, and winning it gave me the money and contacts I needed. I work with three friends from my course, and we share every decision equally. The app now has thousands of users, but it still doesn't make a profit, which keeps me awake at night. We spend most of our time answering emails from users and fixing the problems they report. Our next step is to add Spanish and French, which users ask for every week.
D  Ollie, 24, owns a café that employs young people who have left care
I wanted a business that did some good, not just made money. Every member of staff is someone who grew up in care and found it hard to get a first job. The café struggled at the beginning because the location was poor, so we moved after a year, and that changed everything. People sometimes assume we survive on donations, but we pay our way like any other café, and I'm proud of that. Training new staff takes time and patience, and not everyone stays. But several former employees now run cafés of their own, which matters more to me than any award.

long.title: A Year Abroad: Four Volunteers
long.text:
A  Linh, who taught English in a village school in Nepal
I arrived thinking I would be the teacher, but I learned far more than my pupils did. The school had no electricity for most of the day, so I had to plan lessons that needed nothing but a blackboard and our voices. The families I stayed with treated me like a daughter, and leaving them was the saddest day of the year. I've been back twice since then, and next summer I'm taking my parents to meet them. The children loved learning songs, so we sang in English every morning before lessons. I also learned enough Nepali to chat with the shopkeepers in the village.
B  Marcus, who worked on a turtle conservation project in Costa Rica
Most of the work was at night, walking the beach for hours to protect turtle nests from people who steal the eggs. It was exhausting and sometimes boring, and I almost went home after the first month. What changed my mind was seeing hundreds of baby turtles reach the sea safely. The project made me realise I wanted to study biology, which is what I'm doing now. The volunteers came from more than ten countries, and we lived together in a simple wooden house near the beach. Some of them are still my closest friends.
C  Elena, who helped build houses in Peru
I'd never used a hammer before, and at first I felt useless next to local builders who could do everything twice as fast. The organisation charged volunteers a large fee, and I later discovered that only a small part of it reached the community, which made me angry. I'd tell anyone thinking of volunteering to research the organisation carefully. Even so, I'm proud of the two houses we finished. We lived with local families and worked six days a week alongside people from the community, who taught us everything with great patience.
D  Josh, who worked at a children's hospital in Ghana
I wasn't a doctor or a nurse, so my job was to play with the children and help their parents with practical things. Some days were very hard emotionally. The thing I'm most grateful for is learning to cope without the comforts I'd always taken for granted, such as hot water and a fast internet connection. I came home much more patient than I was when I left. Many of the children had to stay in hospital for months, so the playroom was the most important place in the building for them. I organised games, drawing and, once, a small concert by the children for their parents.

long.title: In Praise of Boredom
long.text:
There was a time, not so very long ago, when boredom was an unavoidable part of daily life. Waiting for a bus, sitting in a doctor's waiting room or enduring a long car journey, people had little choice but to let their minds drift. Today, that empty time has all but disappeared. The moment we have nothing to do, we reach for our phones, and the faint discomfort of having nothing to occupy us is relieved within seconds. Few of us would regard this as a loss. Boredom, after all, is unpleasant. Yet a growing number of psychologists are suggesting that in eliminating it, we may have deprived ourselves of something valuable.
The case for boredom rests largely on what it prompts us to do. In a frequently cited experiment, researchers asked one group of participants to spend fifteen minutes copying numbers from a telephone directory, a task chosen precisely because it was so tedious. Afterwards, both this group and a control group were asked to think of as many uses as possible for a pair of plastic cups. Those who had endured the dull task came up with significantly more ideas, and more original ones. The researchers concluded that boredom pushes the mind to search for stimulation, and that when the outside world provides none, it turns inwards and starts to generate its own.
It would be easy to overstate such findings. Laboratory studies of this kind tend to involve small numbers of participants, usually university students, and some attempts to repeat them have produced weaker results. Moreover, there is a difference between the mild, temporary boredom of a waiting room and the chronic boredom experienced by people trapped in monotonous jobs or isolated by illness, which has been linked to depression and risky behaviour. No one is seriously arguing that the latter should be encouraged.
What the researchers do argue is that the brief, everyday kind of boredom serves a purpose, functioning rather like a signal. Just as hunger tells us to eat, boredom tells us that what we are currently doing is not satisfying, and that we should look for something more meaningful. The difficulty with smartphones, according to this view, is not that they are harmful in themselves but that they silence the signal too quickly. We respond to the discomfort with the easiest available distraction, rather than asking what it might be telling us.
There is also the question of what the mind does when it is left to wander. Neuroscientists have identified a network of brain regions that becomes more active when we are not focused on any particular task. This so-called 'default mode network' appears to be involved in remembering the past, imagining the future and making sense of our own experiences. Some researchers believe that constant stimulation may limit the time this network has to do its work, although they admit that the evidence is still far from conclusive.
None of this means we should throw away our phones. The more modest suggestion is that we might occasionally resist the urge to fill every empty moment. Some schools have experimented with 'quiet time', in which pupils simply sit without books or screens for ten minutes, and teachers report that, after initial complaints, many children come to value it. For adults, the prescription may be as simple as leaving the phone in a pocket on the bus and seeing where our thoughts lead.
Whether this will make us more creative is uncertain. But it seems reasonable to suspect that a mind which is never allowed to be empty may also find it harder to be full.

long.title: How I Became a Scientist
long.text:
A  Dr Ana Ruiz, marine biologist
'I grew up a long way from the sea, so my fascination with it was entirely second-hand: books, documentaries, a poster of a humpback whale above my bed. When I finally saw the ocean at the age of fourteen, I was almost disappointed; it was grey and cold and nothing like the pictures. It took me years to understand that this was the real lesson. Science is mostly about the gap between what you expect and what you actually find. These days I spend months at sea collecting data that rarely confirms what I predicted, and I've come to enjoy that. My one regret is that I didn't study more maths at school. I spent my first year of university desperately catching up.'
B  Professor Kwame Mensah, astronomer
'My route was anything but direct. I trained as an accountant, because my family wanted me to have a secure profession, and I spent six years auditing companies' accounts. Astronomy was a hobby: I had a small telescope on the roof of our flat. What changed things was an online project that invited amateurs to classify galaxies in telescope images. I became rather obsessed, and one of the objects I flagged turned out to be genuinely unusual. The researchers who ran the project encouraged me to apply for a doctorate. I was thirty-one, and I'd be lying if I said I wasn't terrified. Oddly, my accounting background has proved useful. Much of astronomy is about spotting small errors in very large data sets.'
C  Dr Mai Tran, neuroscientist
'I can name the exact moment: a lecture in my second year of a medicine degree, when a professor showed us brain scans of a patient who could recognise objects but not faces. I remember thinking that if the brain could break in such a specific way, it must be organised in a way none of us understood. I switched from medicine to research the following year, which my parents found hard to accept. People imagine research is about brilliant ideas, but most of my week is spent writing applications for funding, and the competition is fierce. I'd tell anyone considering this career to be prepared for rejection. Most of my proposals are turned down, and you have to learn not to take it personally.'
D  Dr Jonas Berg, climate scientist
'I was not a promising student. I left school at sixteen and worked in a ski resort for several years, which, ironically, is how I became interested in climate. The older instructors kept telling me how much the snow had changed since they were young, and I wanted to know whether they were right or simply nostalgic. That question took me back into education through evening classes, and eventually to university. The answer, as it happens, was that they were right. I sometimes think my unconventional background helps when I talk to the public. I know what it's like to be sceptical of experts, and I try to show people the evidence rather than simply asking them to trust me.'

long.title: Should schools set homework?
long.text:
A  Dr Helen Marsh, education researcher
The research on homework is more consistent than the public debate suggests. For students in secondary school, well-designed homework is clearly linked to higher achievement, but the gains stop at around an hour a night; beyond that, extra work adds nothing except anxiety. For younger children, by contrast, there is simply no reliable evidence of benefit, and I see no reason to keep it in primary schools. What matters most is that teachers actually respond to what students produce. Homework that is collected and never discussed teaches pupils only that it does not matter. Schools that have dropped homework in the early years have seen no fall in later results.
B  Mark Davies, headteacher
I have run schools for twenty years, and I am convinced that homework builds the habits of independent study that pupils need later on. That is why I set short reading and spelling tasks even for six-year-olds: the routine is the point. Pupils who arrive at secondary school without that habit, in my experience, struggle for years. Older students certainly benefit too. I am less persuaded by claims that homework ruins family life; most parents I speak to are glad to see what their children are learning. Detailed marking of every task, frankly, matters less than the habit of regular practice.
C  Priya Shah, parent and journalist
In our house, homework has caused more arguments than anything else. Evenings that could be spent playing, reading for fun or simply sleeping are swallowed by worksheets that my children find pointless. I am not convinced that any of it improves results, at any age; the studies I have read seem weak to me, and they rarely measure what children lose. Where homework is genuinely interesting, such as a small research project, my children throw themselves into it, which tells me that the problem is the kind of task we usually give them. When I raised this at a parents' meeting, I discovered that many other families felt exactly the same.
D  Professor Leon Brooks, psychologist
Practising at home helps students to remember what they have learned in class, particularly when the practice is spread over several days, and the evidence for older students is strong. Short, regular tasks are far more effective than a single long assignment at the weekend. Young children are a different matter; I would set them nothing beyond encouraging them to read for pleasure. Above all, homework is wasted unless teachers give feedback on it, because students cannot correct mistakes they do not know they have made. As for stress at home, it is real, but it usually comes from long, poorly explained tasks.

long.title: Is space exploration worth the cost?
long.text:
A  Dr Sarah Lindqvist, astrophysicist
Critics who call space exploration a luxury rarely notice how small the budget is: most space agencies receive less than one per cent of what their governments spend each year. For that modest sum, we have gained satellite weather forecasting, better materials and a much deeper understanding of our own planet. I would, however, send robots rather than people wherever possible. They cost a fraction as much, take no risks with human life and return far more data. Every major advance in our understanding of the solar system over the past forty years has come from robotic probes. I welcome private launch companies, which have already cut the cost of reaching orbit.
B  James Holloway, economist
The familiar argument that space programmes produce useful inventions does not stand up. If a society wants better batteries or medical scanners, it is far cheaper to fund that research directly than to hope it emerges as a by-product of a rocket. Supporters of space programmes always point to a handful of famous inventions, but they never count the far larger number of projects that produced nothing useful at all. With so many urgent problems on Earth, from disease to unsafe drinking water, public money should go there first. I have no objection to private firms spending their own investors' money on rockets; that is their business.
C  Amina Bello, science writer
The technologies developed for space have transformed everyday life, from the cameras in our phones to water purification systems. But the true value of crewed missions lies elsewhere: nothing inspires young people to study science like watching a human being step onto another world, and no robot can do that. When I visit schools, the questions children ask are almost always about astronauts, not about probes or telescopes. What worries me is the growing role of private companies, whose commercial interests do not always match the public good and whose satellites are filling orbit with dangerous debris.
D  Professor Paul Grant, engineer
From an engineering point of view, the case for robotic missions is overwhelming: they are cheaper, more reliable and can go where humans never could. A human crew needs food, water, air and a way home; a robot needs only power and a working radio. Human spaceflight is largely about national prestige. Even so, the knowledge gained in designing spacecraft has changed manufacturing, and private companies are now driving exactly the kind of rapid innovation that state agencies struggled to achieve. Satellites monitoring the climate alone justify much of the spending.

long.title: Working from home: four views
long.text:
A  Rachel Kim, human resources director
In our company, output has stayed the same or risen since most staff began working from home several days a week, and people report a much better balance between work and family. We have also been able to recruit people who live too far away to travel to the office every day. The cost falls on younger employees, who no longer pick up skills by overhearing experienced colleagues and who are noticed less by managers. Offices will become smaller, but they will survive as places where teams meet in person.
B  Dr Omar Farouk, organisational psychologist
People do concentrate better at home on tasks that need focus, but creative work suffers when colleagues never meet by chance. Video calls are useful for planned discussions, but they are a poor substitute for the conversations that happen by the coffee machine. Junior staff in particular lose the informal guidance that once came from sitting near experienced colleagues. I also see the boundary between work and private life disappearing: many people now answer messages late into the evening and end up working longer hours than before. In my view the office remains essential and will not shrink as much as many predict.
C  Tom Reid, owner of a small design business
When my team worked entirely from home, productivity in my firm dropped noticeably, and we now meet in the office three days a week. I was sceptical about the whole idea at first, but our experience has persuaded me that a mixed arrangement works best for a small firm like ours. What surprised me was how well our youngest designers did online. With clear systems, regular video meetings and a mentor assigned to each of them, they learned quickly and spoke up more than they ever had in meetings. We gave up half of our office space last year, and I suspect many firms will do the same. My staff say they have more time for their families.
D  Claire Dubois, economist
The productivity figures are mixed, and anyone who claims certainty either way is reading the evidence selectively. Some studies find small gains, others small losses, and much depends on how output is measured in the first place. What is clearer is that demand for office space will fall sharply, with serious consequences for city centres. Younger workers are the group most likely to lose out, because promotion still depends on being seen. And like many researchers, I find that home workers often end up working longer days, as the time once spent travelling is simply absorbed by work.

long.title: In Praise of Boredom
long.text:
There was a time, not so long ago, when waiting for a bus meant staring at the road. Today, the moment a queue forms, almost everyone in it reaches for a phone. We have, it seems, collectively decided that boredom is a problem to be eliminated, and technology has given us the means to eliminate it entirely. I want to suggest that we may have made a poor bargain.

Boredom has rarely enjoyed a good reputation. Philosophers have described it as a kind of spiritual emptiness, teachers treat it as a sign that a lesson has failed, and parents rush to fill every gap in their children's timetables. Yet psychologists who have studied the experience in recent years have reached a more interesting conclusion. Boredom, they argue, is not simply the absence of stimulation; it is a signal, much like hunger, telling us that what we are currently doing is not satisfying and that we should look for something better.

Seen this way, the trouble with constantly filling empty moments is not that it wastes time, but that it silences the signal before we can act on it. Scrolling through a news feed relieves the discomfort of having nothing to do without ever addressing its cause. We end the day feeling oddly flat, having been occupied for hours without being engaged by anything.

There is also evidence that boredom can be productive. In one frequently cited experiment, participants who first spent fifteen minutes on a deliberately dull task, copying numbers from a telephone directory, then produced more original ideas in a creativity test than those who went straight to it. The researchers suggested that a mind left without stimulation begins to wander, and that this wandering allows unexpected connections to form. Many writers and scientists have described their best ideas arriving not at their desks but during long walks, in the shower or on tedious train journeys.

I do not want to romanticise the experience. Chronic boredom, the kind experienced by people in repetitive jobs or in institutions with nothing to do, is associated with anxiety, depression and risky behaviour, and nobody would wish it on anyone. Nor is every idle moment secretly creative; often the wandering mind simply returns to the same small worries. The point is not that boredom is good in itself, but that brief, ordinary episodes of it seem to serve a purpose that we interrupt at our cost.

Part of the difficulty in following this advice is that modern technology is designed to hold our attention. The apps on our phones are built by teams whose success is measured by how long we stay, and they are extremely good at their jobs. Faced with an endless supply of short, mildly interesting content, a brief spell of boredom has little chance; it is hardly a fair contest, and most of us lose it many times a day. Children, who are given phones at ever younger ages, may have even fewer opportunities to learn what to do with an empty afternoon.

What, then, should we do? Banning phones from bus queues is neither possible nor desirable. A more realistic aim might be to notice the impulse to reach for distraction and occasionally to resist it, to let a few minutes pass without input and see what the mind does with them. Some schools have begun to build short periods of unstructured time into the day, partly to give pupils the chance to discover what they actually want to do. It is a modest experiment, but it reflects a growing recognition that a life without empty moments may also be a life with fewer new thoughts.

long.title: The Restorer's Dilemma
long.text:
When I was asked to lead the restoration of a fourteenth-century castle on the Welsh border, I assumed that the hardest decisions would be technical: how to stabilise walls that had been leaning for six hundred years, or how to stop rainwater seeping into the great hall. In fact the most difficult questions turned out to be philosophical. What, exactly, were we restoring the building to?

A castle like this one is not a single object frozen at one moment in history. It was extended in the fifteenth century, partly demolished during a civil war, converted into a farmhouse in the eighteenth century and finally abandoned in the nineteenth. Each period left marks on the stone: a blocked medieval window here, a Georgian fireplace there, the scars of cannon fire on the eastern tower. To choose one date and rebuild the castle as it supposedly looked at that time would mean destroying the evidence of every other.

The technical work, when it came, was demanding enough. Engineers spent months monitoring the leaning walls with sensors before deciding that they could be held in place with stainless steel ties rather than rebuilt. Ivy, which had been both damaging the stonework and holding parts of it together, had to be removed one section at a time. Every stone that came loose was numbered, recorded and, wherever possible, returned to its original position. Much of this work is invisible to visitors, which is exactly as it should be, and it took almost two years before we could turn to the questions that would prove far harder.

There was considerable pressure to do exactly that. Local businesses wanted a building that looked like a castle in a children's book, complete with battlements, which they believed would attract more tourists. Some members of the funding committee asked whether we could rebuild the collapsed north tower. I understood the appeal, but nobody knew what the tower had looked like, and anything we built would have been a guess presented as history.

The principle we eventually adopted was one that many conservation professionals now share: repair as much as necessary but as little as possible. Where stone had to be replaced to keep a wall standing, we used material from the same quarry and allowed it to show as new rather than ageing it artificially. Visitors can see clearly which parts are original and which are ours. Where we found the Georgian fireplace blocking a medieval doorway, we left both, with a panel explaining the change. The building, in other words, tells its own story, including the parts of the story that are inconvenient.

Not everyone was satisfied. A local newspaper complained that we had spent a great deal of public money on a ruin that still looked like a ruin, and visitor numbers in the first year were lower than the businesses had hoped. I have some sympathy with the disappointment. Ruins are harder to read than complete buildings, and we had perhaps underestimated how much help visitors would need to imagine what had been there.

Our answer was not to rebuild but to explain. We added a small exhibition and a free app that shows, as you walk through the rooms, how each space looked at different periods. Visitor numbers have risen steadily since. I am still convinced that we made the right decision. A restored building that pretends to be something it never was may please visitors for a while, but it deceives them, and it destroys the very evidence that later generations, with better methods than ours, might have used to understand it more fully.

long.title: Where Ideas Come From: Four Artists
long.text:
A  Clara Voss, painter
I distrust the idea of inspiration arriving like a flash of light. My best work comes from routine: I am in the studio at eight every morning, whether or not I feel like painting, and most of what I produce on any given day is unremarkable. Occasionally, though, something unplanned happens on the canvas, and I have learned to recognise those moments and follow them. Young artists often ask me for the secret, and they are visibly disappointed when I tell them it is mostly showing up. I keep a box of failed paintings under the stairs; looking through it reminds me how many wrong turns it takes to find a right one. I also rarely show unfinished work to anyone, not even my family, because early opinions tend to push a painting in a direction it was never meant to take.
B  Daniel Achebe, composer
Much of my music begins with sounds I hear by accident: a lorry reversing, rain on a metal roof, two conversations overlapping on a train. I record them on my phone and listen back weeks later, when I have forgotten where they came from. Collaboration is essential to me; I rarely write anything without first discussing it with the musicians who will perform it, and their suggestions often change a piece completely. I find working alone for long periods quite unhealthy, both for the music and for me. Some of the pieces I am proudest of were written for amateur choirs, whose enthusiasm more than makes up for their limited technique, and who are often braver than professionals.
C  Mira Sato, novelist
Ideas are never my problem; I have notebooks full of them. The difficulty is deciding which ones deserve two or three years of my life. My test is simple: if a character is still on my mind after six months, I start writing. I plan very little in advance and often have no idea how a novel will end until I reach the final chapters, which my publisher finds alarming. Reading outside my own field, especially history and science, feeds my imagination far more than reading other novelists. I write every morning for four hours and spend the afternoons walking, which is usually when problems in the plot quietly solve themselves without my noticing.
D  Paolo Rinaldi, choreographer
I begin with the dancers rather than with an idea. In the first weeks of rehearsal I simply watch how each of them moves and ask them to improvise, and the piece grows out of what I see. For that reason, no two performances of my work are identical, and I like it that way. Criticism used to wound me deeply, but I have come to see a bad review as information rather than judgement. The worst thing an artist can do, I think, is repeat a past success because audiences expect it. Our company tours small towns as well as major theatres, and some of my favourite performances have taken place in school halls, in front of people who had never seen dance before.

long.title: The Museum of the Future: Four Curators
long.text:
A  Hannah Weiss, director of a science museum
Twenty years ago, a museum visit meant walking past glass cases and reading small labels. Now visitors expect to touch, try and take part, and we have redesigned almost every gallery around activities. The change has worked: families stay twice as long as they used to. My concern is that we may have gone too far, and that some of the quieter pleasures of looking closely at a real object are being lost. We are now experimenting with one gallery where nothing at all is interactive. Schools remain our most important visitors, and every new exhibition is now designed together with teachers, who tell us very quickly what children will ignore and what will hold their attention.
B  Kofi Mensah, curator of African art
Museums like mine hold thousands of objects that were taken from their countries of origin during the colonial period, often by force. I believe we have a duty to return those that communities ask for, and we have already sent several collections home. Some colleagues fear that this will empty our galleries, but in practice returns have led to new partnerships, loans and exhibitions that we could never have created alone. The museum of the future will be a meeting place, not a storehouse. Each return involves long discussions with community leaders, historians and governments, and these conversations have taught my staff a great deal about the objects themselves and the people who made them.
C  Lucía Ortega, head of digital collections
Only about five per cent of our collection is ever on display; the rest sits in storage. Photographing and publishing the whole collection online has opened it to researchers and the public across the world, and our online visitors now outnumber those who come through the doors. People sometimes ask whether this will make physical visits unnecessary. I don't think so: in our experience, seeing an object online makes people more, not less, likely to want to see it in person. The project was slower and more costly than we expected, mainly because every object had to be checked, measured and described by a specialist before it could be photographed.
D  James Whitfield, director of a small local museum
Much of the debate about the future of museums is about large national institutions with large budgets. In a small town, our challenge is simply survival. We depend almost entirely on volunteers, and our income comes from the café and a few events each year. What keeps us going is the local community, who bring us objects, photographs and memories. I am wary of expensive technology; a good conversation with a knowledgeable volunteer often means more to visitors than any screen. Last year we held an exhibition of wedding photographs lent by local families, and it attracted more visitors than anything we had ever done before, many of whom had never set foot in the museum.

long.title: Lost and Found in Translation
long.text:
Every translator, sooner or later, is asked the same question: how much is lost in translation? It is usually posed sympathetically, as though the speaker imagines the translator as a kind of removal man, carrying furniture from one house to another and inevitably chipping a few chairs on the way. I have been translating novels for nearly twenty years, and I have come to think the question rests on a misunderstanding. It assumes that the original text contains a fixed quantity of meaning, which can only diminish as it is transferred. In my experience, the process is rather less tidy than that, and considerably more interesting.
Consider the simplest of examples. Vietnamese has no single word for 'you'; speakers choose from a range of terms that indicate age, status and degree of intimacy, and a shift from one to another can signal affection, respect or contempt. An English translator has no equivalent device. Something is indeed lost. But the translator who recognises this is forced to look elsewhere, to the rhythm of a sentence, a choice of verb, a carefully placed silence, in order to convey the shift in the relationship. Done well, the result is not a diminished copy but a different solution to the same problem, one which may draw a reader's attention to the relationship in ways the original, precisely because it was so effortless, did not.
None of this is to deny that some losses are real and irreparable. Wordplay is the most obvious casualty. A pun that depends on two meanings of a single word will rarely survive the journey, and the translator must choose between abandoning it, explaining it in a footnote, which is rather like explaining a joke, or inventing a new pun that does similar work. Each option involves a betrayal of some kind. Poetry presents still greater difficulties, since sound and sense are so closely bound together that to alter one is to alter the other. It is no accident that the most admired translations of poetry are often described as 'versions' rather than translations at all.
What troubles me more than these familiar problems, however, is the assumption, widespread among publishers and reviewers alike, that the best translation is an invisible one. A translation is praised when it 'reads as if it were written in English', which sounds like a compliment but conceals a demand: that the strangeness of the original be smoothed away. A novel set in rural Vietnam, in this view, should feel as comfortable to an English reader as one set in Yorkshire. Yet part of the value of reading in translation lies in encountering ways of thinking and speaking that are not one's own. A translation that removes every trace of the foreign may be fluent, but it is also, in an important sense, dishonest.
The opposite approach has its own dangers. Some translators, anxious to preserve the flavour of the original, produce English so awkward that the reader is constantly reminded of the effort involved, much as an overly elaborate frame distracts from the painting it surrounds. The challenge is to find a middle path: English that is natural enough to be read with pleasure, yet retains enough of the original's character to remind readers that they are, after all, somewhere else.
Cultural references pose a subtler problem. A passing mention of a festival, a dish or a popular song may carry, for its original readers, a whole world of associations that a foreign reader cannot be expected to share. The translator can add a few words of explanation, at the risk of slowing the narrative and patronising the reader, or leave the reference as it stands and trust the reader's curiosity. I have increasingly come to favour the second course. Readers, in my experience, are far more tolerant of not understanding everything than publishers tend to assume, and a little uncertainty can be part of the pleasure of being somewhere unfamiliar.
It is often forgotten, too, that translation can add as well as subtract. Readers of a translated novel sometimes notice qualities that the original audience took for granted, and a skilled translation can reveal patterns in a text that its own author never consciously intended. Several writers I have worked with have told me that reading their book in English showed them something new about it. One remarked, only half joking, that she now preferred my version to her own.
So when I am asked how much is lost in translation, I have learned to answer with another question: how much is found? The answer is rarely 'nothing', and occasionally it is 'more than you might think'.

long.title: Is Ambition Overrated?
long.text:
A  Helen Marsh, novelist
'I distrust the word, frankly. In my experience, the people who describe themselves as ambitious are usually describing a desire for status, which is not at all the same as a desire to do something well. The writers I admire most were driven, certainly, but by curiosity rather than any wish to be admired. That said, I'd be a hypocrite to pretend I'm immune. When my first novel was overlooked for a prize, I sulked for a month. What I've learned since is that external recognition is a poor compass. It arrives late, if at all, and it seldom rewards the work one is proudest of. Prizes are pleasant, but they are decided by a handful of people on a particular afternoon, and I've sat on enough juries to know how arbitrary that can be. The only ambition worth having, I think, is the private one of doing better than last time.'
B  Dr Samuel Okafor, economist
'There is a fashionable view that ambition is somehow toxic, and I think it's largely a luxury of the comfortable. If you grow up, as I did, in a household where every expense had to be weighed, ambition isn't a personality trait; it's a survival strategy. My parents never used the word; they simply assumed we would work harder than anyone else, because nobody was going to hand us anything. The research on this is fairly consistent: people who set high goals for themselves tend, on average, to achieve more and earn more, though, interestingly, they aren't noticeably happier. I don't find that troubling. Happiness was never the point. What does concern me is that the language of balance and wellbeing, however well meant, can end up discouraging young people from poorer backgrounds from aiming as high as their wealthier peers do without a second thought.'
C  Akiko Sato, former Olympic rower
'Ambition got me to the Olympics, and it very nearly destroyed me. For eight years, every decision I made, what I ate, who I saw, when I slept, was measured against a single goal. My coaches talked constantly about mental toughness, but nobody ever talked about what happens afterwards. When I retired at twenty-nine, I had no idea who I was without it, and the year that followed was the hardest of my life. I'm not sure I'd do it again. And yet I can't honestly say I regret it either; I learned things about discipline and endurance that I couldn't have learned any other way. What I'd say to young athletes now is to make sure their sense of themselves rests on more than one thing, so that losing it doesn't mean losing everything.'
D  Professor Elena Varga, psychologist
'Much of the confusion in this debate arises because we use a single word for several different things. Psychologists distinguish between goals that are intrinsic, such as mastering a skill or contributing to a community, and extrinsic ones, such as wealth, fame or status. The evidence suggests that pursuing intrinsic goals is associated with greater wellbeing, whereas the relentless pursuit of extrinsic ones tends to be associated with anxiety, even among people who achieve them. So the useful question is not whether ambition is good or bad, but what one is ambitious for. Interestingly, people are often poor judges of their own motives, and goals that feel intrinsic can turn out, on closer inspection, to be about recognition after all.'

long.title: On Forgetting
long.text:
We tend to speak of forgetting as a failure, a small betrayal by a brain that cannot be trusted to hold on to what matters. We apologise for forgetting names, worry when we cannot recall why we walked into a room, and spend considerable sums on apps and courses that promise to sharpen our memories. Rarely do we stop to ask whether forgetting might be doing something useful, or whether a mind that retained everything would be any better off.

There is, in fact, a famous case that suggests it would not. In the early twentieth century, a Russian journalist came to the attention of the psychologist Alexander Luria because he appeared to remember everything. He could reproduce long tables of numbers years after seeing them once, and recall the exact words of conversations he had barely attended to. Yet his extraordinary memory was far from a blessing. He struggled to follow the meaning of a story because every word called up a cascade of images, and he found it difficult to recognise faces, which change from day to day, because he remembered each version too precisely to see what they had in common. To understand, it seems, we must be able to let details go.

This insight lies at the heart of a growing body of research which treats forgetting not as decay but as an active process. Some neuroscientists now argue that the brain spends considerable energy weakening the connections that hold memories in place, and that it does so selectively. Information that is rarely used fades; information that is repeatedly retrieved grows stronger. The result is a memory tuned less to the past than to the future, preserving what has proved useful and discarding what has not.

Forgetting also appears to help us generalise. A child who has been bitten by one particular dog needs to remember that dogs can bite, not every detail of that afternoon. By losing the specific and keeping the general, the mind turns experience into knowledge that can be applied in new situations. Researchers who build artificial learning systems have observed something similar: programs that memorise their training examples too faithfully often perform badly when faced with anything unfamiliar.

None of this means that every lapse is beneficial. The forgetting associated with illnesses such as dementia is a genuine loss, and the frustration of losing a word in mid-sentence is real enough. Nor does the research suggest that we should stop trying to learn. The point is rather that memory and forgetting work together, and that a system designed to remember everything would be less, not more, intelligent.

There may be a personal dimension, too. People who cannot let go of painful memories, who replay old humiliations and quarrels in vivid detail, often suffer for it. Psychologists have long observed that the ability to allow certain experiences to lose their sharpness is part of recovering from them. Forgiveness, in this sense, may owe something to forgetting, or at least to a softening of the edges that time and a healthy brain provide.

Cultures seem to have understood this long before the neuroscience. Oral traditions, which passed stories from one generation to the next without writing, never preserved every detail of the original telling; each storyteller kept the shape and the meaning of a tale while freely changing its surface. Far from being a weakness, this flexibility allowed stories to survive for centuries, adapting to new audiences while keeping what mattered. Written records, by contrast, preserve everything equally, the trivial alongside the essential, and leave it to the reader to decide which is which. Historians of the distant past often complain that they have too little evidence; those who study the recent past increasingly complain that they have far too much, and no time to read it.

It is worth remembering, then, that the next time a name escapes us, our brains may simply be doing their job. In a world that offers us more information each day than our grandparents encountered in a year, the capacity to discard may be as valuable as the capacity to store. We have built machines that remember everything; perhaps the more human achievement is knowing what to forget.

long.title: The Translator's Invisible Art
long.text:
When a translation is praised, the praise is usually for the author. Reviewers admire the elegance of the prose or the precision of the dialogue, and only occasionally remember that every word they are quoting was chosen not by the writer but by me. I do not resent this; in many ways it is the highest compliment a translator can receive. If readers forget that the book was written in another language, I have done my job. Yet the invisibility of the work hides how many decisions it involves, and how few of them have a right answer.

Consider something as apparently simple as a joke. The novel I am currently translating, from Portuguese, contains a scene in which two characters exchange insults based on a pun that cannot exist in English. I can translate the words literally, in which case the scene makes no sense; I can add a footnote explaining the pun, which kills the humour as effectively as explaining any joke; or I can invent a new pun in English that does a similar job. I have chosen the third option, which means that a few lines of the English novel are, strictly speaking, mine rather than the author's. Some translators would consider this a betrayal. I consider it the only form of faithfulness available.

The problem extends far beyond wordplay. Languages divide the world differently. Portuguese has a word, saudade, for a kind of longing for something absent, perhaps lost for ever, that English can only approach through a phrase. Forms of address carry social information that has no English equivalent; whether a character uses a formal or informal 'you' to another can tell a Portuguese reader everything about their relationship, while an English reader notices nothing. The translator must decide, again and again, whether to preserve the strangeness of the original or to smooth it into something that feels natural.

There is no consensus on how to make that choice. One tradition holds that a translation should read as if it had been written in the target language, so that readers are never reminded of the original. Another insists that a good translation should feel slightly foreign, reminding readers that they are encountering a different culture rather than a version of their own. I find myself moving between the two, sometimes within a single page. Dialogue usually needs to sound natural, because people do not speak in translation; descriptions of a city or a meal can afford to keep a little of their original flavour.

I read every chapter aloud before I send it to the publisher. A sentence can be accurate in every word and still be wrong, because its rhythm stumbles where the original flowed, or because it is half as long as the sentence it replaces and so loses the breathlessness the author intended. Reading aloud exposes these problems in a way that silent reading rarely does, and it is one of the reasons why a chapter that takes me a week to draft may take another week to revise. My partner, who has heard more Portuguese novels in English than anyone should, claims she can tell from the next room whether a chapter is finished.

The working conditions of translators rarely match the importance of these decisions. Most of us are paid by the word, at rates that have barely changed in twenty years, and our names are often missing from the cover. Publishers in the English-speaking world translate remarkably few books, partly because they assume readers are reluctant to buy them. The success of several translated novels in recent years suggests that this assumption may be wrong, and there are signs that attitudes are changing, but slowly.

I am sometimes asked whether machines will soon do my job. Automatic translation has become impressively accurate for instructions, contracts and technical documents, and I use it myself to check my first drafts. But a novel is not a set of instructions. Its meaning lies as much in rhythm, implication and silence as in the dictionary sense of its words, and these are precisely the things a machine handles worst. A program can tell me what a sentence says; it cannot yet tell me what the sentence is doing, or what it would cost to lose.

long.title: First Novels: Four Writers Look Back
long.text:
A  Eleanor Price
My first novel was rejected by eleven publishers, and in retrospect most of them were right to reject it. It was far too long and full of beautiful sentences that did nothing for the story. The twelfth publisher accepted it on condition that I cut a third of it, and I spent a miserable summer doing so. It was the most useful education I have ever had. When I reread the book today I can still see the scars of that editing, but I also see a writer learning, painfully, to trust the reader. I sometimes give the original manuscript to students as an example of what not to do, which they find enormously reassuring. The book eventually found a small but loyal readership, mostly through public libraries, and it is still in print more than twenty years later, which nobody, least of all the eleven publishers, predicted.
B  Samuel Okonjo
I wrote my first novel in the evenings while working as a hospital porter, and I had no idea whether it was any good, because I showed it to nobody. That secrecy was a mistake. When it was finally published, a reviewer pointed out a flaw in the plot so obvious that I could not believe I had missed it, and any friend could have spotted it in an afternoon. The book sold modestly, but it was translated into several languages, which surprised me, and a reader in Brazil still writes to me every year. I now ask at least three people to read every draft. Night shifts, oddly, were ideal for writing: the corridors were quiet after two in the morning, and I filled notebook after notebook between calls to move patients from one ward to another.
C  Ingrid Holm
I was thirty-eight when my first novel came out, and I had spent fifteen years writing short stories that no one wanted. People assume that the novel was my breakthrough, but in fact it was those years of failure that made it possible; every technique I used had been tested, and usually spoiled, in a story first. The book did unexpectedly well, which brought its own problems. For two years I could not write anything, because every sentence seemed to be competing with the success of the first book. I would advise new writers to start the next book before the first one is published. The short stories that nobody wanted at the time have since been collected and published, and some readers now tell me, rather to my embarrassment, that they prefer them to the novels.
D  Rafael Moreno
My first novel was largely autobiographical, which is common, and which caused trouble I had not anticipated. Members of my family recognised themselves in characters I had believed were thoroughly disguised, and one of my brothers did not speak to me for a year. I do not regret writing it, but I would handle it differently now. The experience also taught me that readers are much less interested in whether a story really happened than writers imagine; what matters to them is whether it feels true. My later books, which are entirely invented, have been praised for their honesty, which I find rather amusing. I did show the manuscript to my mother before it was published, and she said nothing at all about it, which I mistakenly took as a sign of approval rather than of shock.

long.title: Four Mountaineers Remember
long.text:
A  Thomas Berg
The climb people ask me about is the one that made my name, but the expedition I think about most is one we abandoned four hundred metres below the summit. The weather was turning, and one of our team was showing early signs of altitude sickness. Turning back was the hardest decision I have ever made, and for months afterwards I wondered whether I had been a coward. I now believe it was the best decision of my career. Two members of another team who continued that day did not come home. Since then I have measured a successful expedition by whether everyone returns, not by whether we reach the top. These days I spend more time teaching young climbers to read the weather than climbing high peaks myself. If I can pass on one lesson, it is that the mountain will still be there next year.
B  Aiko Tanaka
I came to climbing late, at thirty-four, after a career in banking, and I have never quite lost the sense that I am an outsider in the climbing world. That has its advantages. I approach each expedition like a business project, with detailed budgets and contingency plans, and some of the more romantic climbers I have worked with found this faintly ridiculous until it saved them. On one expedition our supplies were delayed for a week, and the only reason we could continue was that I had paid for a reserve stock in advance. My former colleagues assumed I had given up a secure life for a reckless hobby. In truth, I take fewer risks on a mountain than I ever took with other people's money, because the consequences of a mistake are so immediate.
C  Grace O'Neill
What I remember most vividly is not any summit but the silence. On one long climb in Alaska we spent nine days on a single face, and for much of that time the only sounds were our breathing and the wind. I had expected to find the isolation frightening; instead, it was the most peaceful I have ever felt. Coming home was harder than the climb itself. The noise and speed of ordinary life overwhelmed me for weeks, and I am not sure the people around me ever understood why. Since then I have climbed in smaller, quieter places rather than chasing famous summits, and I have written two books about solitude in the mountains, which to my publisher's surprise have sold rather well.
D  Viktor Lenz
I have climbed with the same partner for twenty-two years, and I would not attempt a serious route with anyone else. On a mountain you have to know, without speaking, what the other person will do, and that kind of understanding takes years to build. I worry about the commercial expeditions that now take paying clients to the highest peaks. Many of those clients have never climbed together before, and some have barely climbed at all, and they depend entirely on guides who cannot possibly watch everyone at once. My partner and I have turned back from many routes together without a word of argument, because each of us trusts the other's judgement completely. That kind of trust is worth more than any equipment you can buy. Younger climbers sometimes ask me how to find a partner like mine, and I tell them to start on small routes and to be very patient.

wf.text: How long does it take to become an expert? A widely quoted figure suggests ten thousand hours of practice, but this number has been greatly {1}.
